transcript:
Meeting header: Date/Time: 2025-02-19 09:00 UTC / Duration: ~62m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SRE), Samir (Arbor Head of ML), Maya (CTO), Ethan (Platform)
Shared artifacts referenced: throughput-plan.xlsx (internal), redwood-scheduler-guide.pdf (link), arbor-prompt-samples.zip (uploaded)

00:00:12 Alex (Redwood AE): okay everyone, thanks for joining, want to deep dive into throughput tuning — specifically continuous batching and the knobs we've seen customers tweak. I'll hand over to Priya for the se bits.
00:00:28 Priya (Redwood SE): cool, thanks Alex. quick agenda: continuous batching behavior, max_num_seqs tradeoffs, token caps / guardrails, k v cache interactions and quant effects, and finally on-prem / VPC considerations. we'll go slow and take questions.
00:01:05 Samir (Arbor): sounds good. our main pain: spikes during nightly inference jobs push p99 way up and we also have cost concerns. We run mixed short chat requests and long summarization flows.
00:01:26 Priya (Redwood SE): perfect context. so first—continuous batching tries to fill a GPU batch window by holding open calls for up to batch_timeout_ms, then dispatch. default behavior is latency-first for interactive tiers and throughput-first for background tiers.
00:01:58 Ethan (Arbor): is that batch timeout configurable per-route?
00:02:06 Priya: yes per-route and per-model. We also have a scheduler priority layer — per-tenant priority weight and preemption thresholds. if a high-priority interactive request arrives it can preempt filling slots reserved for background jobs, but we enforce token-guard windows to avoid starvation.
00:02:35 Maya (CTO): can you explain token guards? I heard about max_tokens_per_request but not guard windows.
00:02:44 Priya: sure — two concepts: one is per-request token cap (max_tokens) and the other is batch-level token budget or token-guard. The latter prevents a single long sequence from occupying more than x% of batch cycles. practically we set a per-seq token threshold and a per-batch token cap. e.g., max_num_seqs=128 but token-guard=0.25 means no single seq will consume >25% of the token budget.
00:03:20 Samir: ah ok that would help our long-summarize flows from stomping the p99 for interactive chat.
00:03:28 Alex: quick caveat — if you lower max_num_seqs you can increase scheduler dispatch frequency which reduces queueing latency but increases per-token compute overhead (less efficient kernel occupancy). so cost vs latency tradeoff.
00:03:48 Jordan (Redwood SRE): Also note multi-tenant packing means we pack many smaller seqs from different customers - that can help utilization, but fairness is enforced by weights and packing limits to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
00:04:05 Ethan: what's a realistic max_num_seqs for gen-2 models on A100?
00:04:12 Priya: depends on sequence lengths. for median seq length 32 tokens, we've seen max_num_seqs 128-256 yields best throughput on A100 80GB. for median seq 256 tokens, 32-64 is better. there's a sweet spot you must benchmark.
00:04:35 Samir: can you give numbers? ballpark p50/p99 with and without k v cache?
00:04:42 Priya: rough numbers from internal bench — baseline single-tenant: seq_len=32, max_num_seqs=256 => throughput ~12k tokens/s, p99 ~45ms. with kv cache warm and 85% hitrate latency drops to p99 ~28ms because we avoid recompute and reduce memory traffic. with seq_len=256 and max_num_seqs=64 throughput ~9k tokens/s but p99 goes up to ~120-180ms if cache miss heavy. these are illustrative.
00:05:25 Maya: kv cache hit-rate depends on prefix reuse patterns I guess?
00:05:31 Priya: exactly. For chat-like workload where users contextually continue, prefix/KV hit rate is high. For one-off summarization, it's low. We recommend prefix caching for user sessions and also pre-warming for scheduled jobs.
00:05:48 Samir: what about quantization? we tried 4-bit and saw slower tail sometimes.
00:05:55 Priya: right—quantization reduces memory and can enable higher effective batch sizes but changes kernel selection. some 4-bit kernels have higher per-token latency for short sequences because they don't vectorize small token workloads as well. 8-bit or mixed-int8 often gives better p99 for small seqs, while 4-bit shines when you can increase batch size and saturate GPU. so you must balance quant profile with expected seq length distribution.
00:06:28 Ethan: so perhaps we should use dynamic quant profiles per route?
00:06:34 Priya: yes that's supported — route-level quantization policy. we can route interactive chat to int8 profile and background summarization to int4 for cost savings. There is also runtime fallback: if a model variant is incompatible it can fallback to higher-precision model to meet latency SLO.
00:06:55 Jordan: we also touched on scheduler knobs we can tune: max_num_seqs, batch_timeout_ms, max_tokens_per_batch, preempt_threshold_ms, fair_share_window. all of these are in the scheduler JSON we shared.
00:07:15 Samir: what's preempt_threshold_ms?
00:07:19 Priya: it's the time window where a higher priority request will preempt a batch that hasn't started processing yet. small values reduce latency for new high-priority requests but can hurt throughput because of broken batches. common values: 2-8ms for interactive tiers.
00:07:36 Maya: any gotchas on VPC / on-prem?
00:07:42 Alex: networking can change effective batch timeout decisions. on a VPC with inter-node RPC for shared KV cache you may see additional RTT that makes small batch timeouts counterproductive. also on-prem with limited PCIe bandwidth between host and GPU you may hit memory transfer bottlenecks. we usually recommend running a small microbench in-customer to measure host->GPU transfer times and network RTT before picking knobs.
00:08:10 Ethan: how does KV cache topology work in private mode? is it per-instance or centralized?
00:08:16 Priya: in hosted we use a distributed KV cache with local fill and background replication. in private (VPC/on-prem) you can choose local per-node cache (fastest) or a centralized cache service. centralized simplifies consistency across nodes but adds network hops. tradeoff: central cache reduces memory footprint but can increase miss penalty.
00:08:40 Samir: we plan to run private deployment on-prem. can Redwood's scheduler run cross-node packing?
00:08:48 Jordan: cross-node packing isn't recommended because packing assumes low-latency memory sharing; we only pack within a GPU or GPU group. cross-node batching would add synchrony and negates the speed. If you have many small requests across nodes, better to route them to a single pooling node or use our dedicated pooling instance.
00:09:09 Maya: does preemption require kernel aborts? any overhead?
00:09:15 Priya: preemption happens before dispatch — we avoid aborting in-flight kernels. if a pending batch is preempted while waiting we requeue work; cost is mostly wasted fill time but we don't interrupt a kernel mid-execution. mature kernels don't support fast interrupt.
00:09:33 Samir: let's talk about fairness — we have multiple teams and want to protect critical flows. how to ensure background jobs can't starve interactive?
00:09:41 Priya: set per-route priority and a fair_share_window that prevents the scheduler from allocating below baseline for a route. e.g., guarantee 20% cycles to interactive routes. Also token-guards prevent single long jobs from using up the token budget. We can simulate policy with synthetic load and show you the fairness curve.
00:10:05 Ethan: what's typical batch_timeout_ms you recommend for mixed workloads?
00:10:09 Priya: for mixed interactive + background we often use adaptive batch_timeout: start at 8ms, degrade to 20ms under low load. That way when load is light you don't add too much latency but when load increases you collect larger batches.
00:10:26 Alex: quick interjection — adaptive batch timeout is implemented as exponential backoff in the scheduler; it reacts to measured queue fill rates. It's very effective for diurnal workloads.
00:10:40 Samir: ok helpful. can you walk through an example config and what effects changing max_num_seqs has?
00:10:48 Priya: sure — example: config A: max_num_seqs=64, batch_timeout_ms=10, quant=int8, token-guard=0.2. Under mixed short-requests this yields lower p50/p99 but lower throughput per-GPU. Config B: max_num_seqs=256, batch_timeout_ms=20, quant=int4, token-guard=0.25 yields significantly higher tokens/sec but p99 for short requests climbs because we wait longer for batch fill. We provided a CSV in throughput-plan.xlsx with sample runs.
00:11:28 Maya: what's the best way to find our sweet spot?
00:11:31 Priya: iterate: 1) capture request trace and seq length distribution; 2) run 3 bench configs (low-latency, balanced, max-throughput) with your prompt set; 3) measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens; 4) pick a config and then do a short pilot for a week. Redwood can help run steps 2-3.
00:11:52 Samir: hope that's not too heavy operationally.
00:11:56 Alex: we can run the microbench for you with a small dataset — it's part of the pilot. we'll need your anonymized prompts and expected SLOs.
00:12:03 Ethan: for on-prem we have nodes with 4 x 40GB GPUs, 1U servers networked over 25Gb. Anything special there?
00:12:10 Jordan: 25Gb is okay but watch for PCIe host-GPU transfer. Pack small seqs onto a single GPU to avoid cross-GPU comms. Also set max_num_seqs so you don't exceed GPU memory even with kv cache overhead. If you use per-node local cache, memory overhead per GPU increases ~10-15% depending on kv indexing.
00:12:31 Maya: what about throttles and token limits per tenant for safety?
00:12:36 Priya: we support per-tenant rate limits and token quotas; you can set soft limits with alerts and hard caps that reject requests. For bursty workloads enable token-burst windows so allowed bursts consume a separate budget to avoid immediate rejections.
00:12:52 Samir: question about cold starts — we see slow tails when warmup not present. any quick mitigations?
00:12:58 Priya: pre-warm GPU cache, keep a small pool of always-on replicas (steady-state capacity), or use model snapshot warmers that load KV cache entries proactively. For scheduled jobs you can schedule a pre-warm job before run.
00:13:12 Ethan: is KV cache persisted across process restarts in private mode?
00:13:18 Priya: yes we support persistent caches backed by local SSD or networked KV stores; persistence reduces cold-miss penalty but needs reconciliation logic for cache invalidation.
00:13:30 Samir: excellent. can you also share recommended observability checks to validate config changes in production?
00:13:36 Alex: yes — watch p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, batch fill ratio, kv cache hit rate, queue length, and per-route utilization. We also suggest synthetic canaries and alert when p99 > threshold for >5 minutes.
00:13:53 Maya: ok let's talk down to knobs — what's the initial config you'd recommend for us?
00:13:59 Priya: given your mixed workloads and on-prem specifics, start with: max_num_seqs=128, batch_timeout_ms=12, quant=int8 for interactive routes and int4 for background, token-guard=0.2, preempt_threshold_ms=4, fair_share_window=30s. Run a 48h pilot and then evaluate.
00:14:22 Samir: sounds reasonable. we'll provide traces.
00:14:26 Alex: next steps recap — Redwood will run three bench configs on our infra and share CSVs; Samir/Ethan will upload anonymized prompt traces; Jordan will prepare the scheduler JSON and a short notes doc.
00:14:42 [laughter] Speaker 5: thanks everyone.
00:14:50 Alex: one more gotcha—embedding/embedding-like jobs sometimes produce very long token streams; treat them as batch jobs and route to background tier with stronger max_tokens caps.
00:15:07 Priya: also note that some model variants have different KV index formats — mixing types in the same instance can increase memory fragmentation; prefer homogeneous quant/model families per node.
00:15:25 Maya: any compliance/LLP concerns for on-prem?
00:15:30 Alex: you control the private cloud and keys, we offer KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging. We'll share a security checklist.
00:15:38 Samir: great. last question: can we do dynamic route switching based on observed latency? e.g., if p99 > 300ms, switch to lower-latency model?
00:15:47 Jordan: yes — Redwood's routing policies support SLA-based fallbacks and automated route switching. We'll include an example fallback policy in the scheduler JSON.
00:16:00 Priya: okay i'll stop talking now; open floor for quick clarifs.
00:16:05 Ethan: quick one — where do we set token-guard? is it per-model or per-route?
00:16:10 Priya: per-route. you can override per-model defaults.
00:16:15 Samir: thanks, that clarifies.
00:16:20 Alex: wrap-up: we'll send the benchmark plan and scheduler sample; follow-up meeting week of March 3rd. Thanks all.
00:16:32 [meeting ends early but participants stayed for informal follow-up chat]

Informal follow-up (notes):
00:48:00 Samir: we should try int8 for chat first, int4 for nightly summarization.
00:49:15 Priya: agreed — we'll prepare sample config and note expected cost deltas.
00:51:00 Ethan: also interested in per-route alerts for kv cache hit rate < 50%.
00:52:10 Jordan: noted. We'll include that in monitoring dashboard templates.

End of transcript.
